Email production · the design step

How we design emails

What we actually did for the emails, 9–10 Oct 2026, written down so the design step can run inside the chain every week. Every email is a short landing page: thought through, laid out, pictured, checked, then built for Klaviyo.

Calendar→Copy→Design · 6 steps→Approval page→Klaviyo draft→A person schedules
How it runs now · both brands

the team presses one button. the team refines. Done.

1

the team: approve the sends on the calendar board, press "Write the copy"

the team

The calendar has already placed every send: the main sends, the promo sends and the cultural sends for the avatar, each marked designed or letter. Her one button runs the whole line for the sends she picked.

Calendar board: localhost:8790 (components/marketing-calendar)
2

The chain does the rest, by itself

No one

Copy (13 writing steps) → the moment's research and world on a moment send → the job card and concept → the layout from the brand's look and visual DNA, every person and product from the real index first → the key visual and gift pictures made through the image engine and judged → the Klaviyo build with tracking → the product check and the final check. Every step reads the learnings.

3

the team: open the approval page, refine, approve

the team

Each email is already designed, shown exactly as it will arrive. Per email she either presses Approve (it becomes a Klaviyo draft), or Redo with a note (her note becomes a rule for every email after this one, and this email is redone with it), or Send back (the reason is recorded). Final touches happen in the Klaviyo draft; a person presses Schedule.

Approval page: localhost:8798 (tools/email-production/approve_klaviyo.py)
4

It compounds

The learnings

Every correction and every win, from anyone, becomes a DO or a NEVER that every later run reads: shared rules reach every brand and every line (emails, ads, video frames), and a brand's own file holds only its facts. 12 rules are in from today's review, starting with "a tube is never a jar".

runs/learnings/_all.jsonl · runs/learnings/<brand>.jsonl · components/run-kit/run_kit/learnings.py
The line

Six steps, in order

A step starts only when the one before it has its OK. Two steps are yours to OK; the rest the machine checks and shows you only what fails.

1

Think: a job card per email

You OK it, with the layout

Who reads it (segment, what he already believes) · its one job · the one belief it must create · what proves it · the one action · how we'll know · what was cut and why · the product facts it must get right.

runs/email-production//week-2026-10-12/layouts.py · halloween_layouts.py
1b

Concept: never generic

Machine holds any email without one

One concept per email, borrowed from the reader's own culture: read his sub-avatar's culture map, borrow a format he already watches (a horror poster, a barbershop at midnight, a group chat). Written on the card as concept (what he sees) and culture (where it came from). A season gets its own colours.

brands/<brand>/core-avatars/<avatar>/culture-map.md · THEMES in design_system.py
2

Layout: sections top to bottom, no pictures

Your OK

A phone-scale wireframe. The first screen is marked: everything above it must do the whole job alone. Each box says its words and where its picture will come from: type, pull from what we own, real product cut-out, make from a real reference, or ornament.

3

Pictures: real first, made last

Your OK

Every slot filled in this order: the real product → proof we own → made from a real reference. Made pictures get every label read, and a wrong label is fixed by an edit pass on that picture, never a re-roll.

tools/asset-index/machine/proof.py (535 pieces of proof indexed) · social_pull.py
4

Product check

Machine, problems shown to you

Every product picture against the real product · every price against the offer bank · every claim against the product file and position.md's NEVER list · what's in the box against the product file.

5

Build, final check, approve

Your click makes a Klaviyo draft

The designed sections are cut into crisp pictures in the brand's own fonts; letters, buttons, GIFs and footer stay live text; every link carries tracking. A final check runs on every email: links answer, subject and preview set, unsubscribe present, alt text, nothing over 1MB, no customer face twice in a week. Then the card goes on the Klaviyo approval page. Approve makes a draft, never a send; a person presses Schedule.

Pictures

Where every picture comes from, in this order

Real product, cut out

Store 360° frames for NOVA, real packshots for the bottles. Never the 3D model in an email (not production-ready yet).

Brand photo we own

Studio lifestyle shots: in hand with foam, under water, on its base.

Real customer proof

Before/afters, photo reviews, UGC, our own social posts. Used as they are, never made.

Made, from a real reference

Only what nothing we own shows. Real product photo in as the reference, then every label read.

Ornaments from the brand's own set

Made on Higgsfield from crops of the real studio set (gold arch wall, emerald plinth): arch crown behind the logo, emerald rule between sections, deco fan in letters, gold seal on the guarantee only, gold corners on quotes, plinth under the footer. Gold and emerald are for ornaments; the button stays sage.

Rules that came out of your reviews

What every email has to pass

Headline, then its picture

A picture never sits above its headline. A badge or seal is never the opener; it sits with what it proves.

One price, one offer, one button

Lead with the page price; the one-delivery price struck through. Never a deadline the offer doesn't have.

One type system

Serif display only inside pictures. Live text in one sans. Display 34/26/21, body 16, labels 10.5 caps.

Slim header, real logo

The brand's actual logo file, a tight band. No tall header eating the first screen.

No face twice in a week

A customer's photo once a month at most. His words only ever sit with his own face.

Crops show what they name

"Thick at the top" must show the top bristles. Look at every crop before it ships.

Borrow a format, never a person

A homage shows no real face. The villain is the problem, never the man.

The product behaves like itself

NOVA is in a hand, its base or its case, never loose. The case is sold separately, so it never looks like it's in the box.

Subject names the concept

Not the product. Body is two or three short lines in his voice, about the moment.

# Design step 0 · the moment world

PRODUCT TRUTH IS LAW: every product appears exactly as its product file describes it (its container, colour,
proportion and how it is held); never call it or draw it as anything else.

THE EXAMPLES BELOW ARE INVENTED. They show the shape of an answer, never its content. Every scene,
object, format and feeling you write comes from the INPUTS: this reader's culture map, her profile, and
the research on this moment. If an input does not show it, it does not go in.

A send on a moment (a holiday, a sale weekend, a season) has to feel like that moment for THIS reader,
the way the brand's Halloween emails became a horror poster, a barbershop at midnight and a coffin box
(the owner, 2026-10-17: "what is this woman experiencing on Black Friday? She's shopping, she's looking for
gifts, go deep into the research, understand what this person is actually doing … think through the
process of unique elements to really showcase this period of time"). You are writing the moment's world
once, so every email in that moment draws from it.

## INPUTS

<learnings>
{learnings}
</learnings>
LEARNINGS are every correction and every win from past reviews. They outrank everything below except
PRODUCT TRUTH: a NEVER never happens again, a DO always does.

{moment}
</moment>

<moment_research>
{research}
</moment_research>

<avatar_profile>
{avatar}
</avatar_profile>

<culture_map>
{culture}
</culture_map>

<brand_position>
{position}
</brand_position>

<product_truth>
{product_truth}
</product_truth>

## WRITE THESE SECTIONS, in this order, plain words

## HER {moment} — hour by hour
Where she is and what she is doing across the moment, in order (the night before, the day, the days
after), 8 to 12 lines, each one a concrete scene with where it comes from in the inputs.

## THE OBJECTS
15 to 25 real objects from her version of this moment that a picture could hold (the list on the fridge,
the flyer, the gift bag, the remote on the arm of the chair). Each with its source line.

## THE FORMATS SHE WATCHES AND SHARES
The post and video formats of this moment in her feeds and on her TV, each with its source and size.

## WHAT SHE FEELS
The pulls and tensions of the moment for her (buying for everyone but herself, the photos, the
overload), each with its source.

## CONCEPT SEEDS
8 to 12 concepts an email could be built as. Each is ONE line in this exact shape:
`seed name — the borrowed format or scene — how the product enters it (shown, never listed) — source`
A seed borrows a format or a scene she knows, never a real person's face or name. The villain is the
problem, never her. Products are SHOWN inside the scene (in her gift bag, on her list, under the tree),
never as a plain product shot.

## THE BLOW-OUT (key visuals)
A moment email opens on a KEY VISUAL, not a snapshot: a designed picture made to stop the scroll, the
way the brand's Halloween became an 80s horror movie poster with the product as the hero, and its
gift set became five spooky product pictures (the owner, 2026-10-17: "the design and images themselves need
to feel like a blow out too"). Write 6 to 8 key-visual directions for this moment, each ONE line in this
shape:
`key visual name — the borrowed format at full scale (a movie poster, a magazine cover, a flyer's front
page, a TV title card, a gift reveal) — how the real product is the STAR of it — the moment's colours
and light (dramatic, celebratory, maximal within the brand) — the title type the format carries, if any`
Then 4 to 6 GIFT PICTURES: the real products made into this moment's objects (wrapped, tagged, in the
bag, under the tree, in the stocking), each as its own picture.

## PICTURE DIRECTION
For the supporting story pictures (not the key visual): the light, the palette, the props and the places
that make a picture read as this moment for her, and what never appears (the generic version of this
moment every other brand sends).

## THE GENERIC VERSION, BANNED
The tropes every other brand uses for this moment (for a sale weekend: percentage-off badges, SALE
stamps, clip-art shopping bags, countdown clocks with no real deadline). None of them may appear.

Invented example of ONE seed line, for the SHAPE only:
`the porch drop-off — a package left on the welcome mat in the cold — the tube is what's inside the box she opens — profile §5`

# Design step 1 + 1b · the job card and the concept

BRAND VISUAL DNA: the signature elements that make this brand look like itself; every email uses them.
PRODUCT TRUTH IS LAW: every product appears exactly as its product file describes it (its container, colour,
proportion and how it is held); never call it or draw it as anything else.

THE EXAMPLES BELOW ARE INVENTED. They show the shape of an answer, never its content. Every
word you write comes from the INPUTS: this brand, this product, this reader, this culture map.
Never borrow a product, a person, a price, a place or a joke from an example.

You are planning ONE email before anyone designs it (the owner, 2026-10-09: "think from a
first-principles perspective about the designs of these emails and what needs to actually go
in them"). The copy is already written and signed off. Your job is to decide what this email
must do, and the one concept from the reader's own culture that makes it impossible to mistake
for every other email he gets.

## INPUTS

## FILL EVERY SLOT. One line each unless the slot says otherwise.

READER: who opens this (the segment, and the avatar's own profile) and what he or she already believes about us.
JOB: the email's one job, in one sentence.
BELIEF: the one belief it has to create.
PROOF: what proves it, from what the brand owns (a real customer, a real result, the product's
  own facts). Never a statistic the copy does not carry.
ACTION: the one action. One button.
MEASURE: how we will know it worked.
CUT: what from the copy or the obvious design you are leaving out, and why.
PRODUCT_FACTS: every price, product name, claim and in-the-box fact this email must get exactly
  right, each with where it comes from in the inputs.
CONCEPT: one line, what the reader SEES. A format borrowed from the culture map (a poster, a
  show, a group chat, a ritual, a place), never a real person's face, name or likeness. The
  villain is the problem, never the reader.
CULTURE: the format borrowed and the exact line of the culture map it comes from, quoted.
THEME: REQUIRED when the send's `occasion` is a named moment (a holiday, a sale event such as
  black-friday or cyber-monday, a season): the moment's key, taken from BRAND MOMENT LOOKS when the
  brand has one for it. When the brand has no look for that moment, still write the moment's key: the
  line holds the email until the look is made. `none` only for a send on no moment.
SUBJECT: a subject line that names the concept, not the product. 30 to 50 characters.
PREVIEW: the preview line, 30 to 50 characters.
OPEN_QUESTION: anything only a person can decide (who signs it, a fact that is not on file), or
  `none`.

## RULES (each one came from a review)

1. A letter is a note from a person: one photo, three or four short paragraphs, one ask. A
   design email is a short landing page: five to eight pictures, no block over 30 words.
   Follow the KIND you are given; do not change it.
2. Lead with the page price the inputs give; the one-delivery price struck through. Never a
   deadline the offer does not have.
3. One price, one offer, one button.
4. Nothing in the brand design rules may be broken by the concept.
5. If the copy has no product, the concept still comes from the culture map.
6. A send on a moment is built from the MOMENT WORLD: the concept is one of its seeds or is made from its
   scenes and objects, and it must FEEL like that moment on its first screen: the concept lives inside the
   moment (Black Friday is an event, after dark, the one weekend of the year), the eyebrow names it,
   the hero picture is set in it. A concept that would read the same on any ordinary week has failed.
7. Never a concept already used in this batch: each email in a run gets its own borrowed format.

## ANSWER

Return ONLY a JSON object with the slots above as lower-case keys (`reader`, `job`, `belief`,
`proof`, `action`, `measure`, `cut`, `product_facts` as a list of strings, `concept`, `culture`,
`theme`, `subject`, `preview`, `open_question`). No prose before or after it.

Invented example of the SHAPE only:
{"reader": "Bought once, months ago; thinks it was fine but forgot it.", "job": "...", "belief": "...", "proof": "...", "action": "...", "measure": "...", "cut": "...", "product_facts": ["..."], "concept": "...", "culture": "...", "theme": "none", "subject": "...", "preview": "...", "open_question": "none"}

</brand_design_rules>

## HOW TO LAY IT OUT

1. FIRST SCREEN. The top ~560px (header + the first section or two) must do the whole job
   alone: the headline, its picture right after it, and for a design email the price and the
   button. A headline is followed straight away by its picture; a picture never sits above its
   headline. A badge or seal is never the opener.
2. KIND. A letter: `mark`, then `letter` (greeting + three or four short paragraphs from the copy),
   at most one picture (a `hero_photo` or an `example`), one `cta`, `sign`, `foot`. A design email:
   `band`, a `hero_type` or `hero_photo`, then the format's sections, ending on a `product` card
   or the `guarantee`, then `foot`. Never both kinds in one email.
3. WORDS. Use the copy's own words. Cut, never add a claim. No block over 30 words in a design
   email. The headline may carry one accent word in <i>…</i>.
4. PICTURES, in this order, for every slot:
   a. the real product: `{"stage": "product:<name>"}` or `{"glow": "product:<name>"}`, names from
      REAL PRODUCT PICTURES only;
   b. real proof the brand owns: `{"proof": "<id>"}`, ids from REAL PROOF only (each line says what is IN
      the picture: the shot, the person and her age, which product she holds, quality, baked-in words).
      EVERY PERSON IN THE EMAIL IS A REAL ONE FROM THIS LIST: a real customer holding the real tube beats any
      made picture. Pick quality 4-5, words none, the person matching the reader; a customer's
      words sit only with that customer's own picture; never a picture listed as used elsewhere;
   c. a photo the brand owns: `{"photo": "<ref>", "ratio": 0.8, "focus": [0.5, 0.4]}`, refs from BRAND PHOTOS
      WE OWN only (lifestyle, packshot, texture, ingredients, customer posts), cropped to the slot;
   d. only then a picture to make: `{"todo": "<what it shows>", "brief": "<the picture brief: the
      shot, the real reference it starts from, which real product is in it>", "use": "key-visual" | "gift" |
      "story", "product": "<name from REAL PRODUCT PICTURES, or omit>"}`. `use` is what the picture is
      for: the email's opening blow-out (key-visual), a real product made into the moment's object (gift),
      or a documentary moment from her day (story). A key visual's brief names its format, its drama, its
      colours and, when the format carries a title, the exact words of that title.
   Every picture carries `"alt"` (what is in it, plainly) and `"source"`: `cut` | `proof` | `photo` | `make`.
   Show, don't list: anything the email names (each product in a set) gets its own picture.
   The product behaves like itself: held, in use, or on its own stand, never loose.
5. THEME. Use the job card's theme (`null` when it says none).
5a. THE BLOW-OUT. A moment email opens on a KEY VISUAL from the MOMENT WORLD's blow-out list, set as a
   full-bleed `poster` section right under the band (or as the picture of a `hero_overlay`): a designed
   picture with the moment's energy, the borrowed format at full scale, the real product as its star; its
   brief names the format, the drama, the colours and any title type the format carries. Add a `ticker`
   band (the moment's words repeating) under it, at least one GIFT PICTURE section (`box` or `tiles`: each
   real product made into the moment's object), and big type. A moment email is loud and celebratory
   within the brand: never a quiet ordinary-day email in a dark frame.
5b. THE MOMENT. On a moment send, every other picture to make is a scene or an object from the MOMENT WORLD
   (its hour-by-hour scenes, its objects, its picture direction), never an ordinary day: the hero is her
   in the moment, and the products appear INSIDE the moment (in the gift bag, on the list, under the
   tree), each as its own made picture from the real product photo. Nothing from its banned generic
   version appears.
6. Respect every brand design rule; a banned picture idea is never used.

## COMPOSITION (you are an expert designer; this is how the brand's best emails are built)

- 8 to 11 sections. One idea per section; nothing repeats an idea already made.
- The rhythm of a selling email: key visual → (ticker on a moment) → the offer and the one button on the
  first screen → the proof (a real customer and her own words) → the product and its texture → the
  ingredients → the set as gift pictures (on a moment) → the guarantee → footer.
- Never two text-only sections in a row; never more than one dark panel; the same section type never twice
  in a row. Every section either carries a picture or is a single deliberate type moment.
- One alignment for the whole email (the brand's), one button style, the same picture corner and spacing
  throughout. Words are short: headlines up to 7 words, body up to 2 short lines per section.
- Use the brand's signature formats from its VISUAL DNA (e.g. the ingredient card, the tube in its mound,
  real customers holding the tube) before inventing new ones.

## ANSWER

Return ONLY one JSON object, the email's spec:

{"kind": "design" | "letter", "theme": null | "<theme>", "subject": "...", "preview": "...",
 "sections": [ {"s": "<section name>", ...that section's fields...}, ... ],
 "notes": ["one line per decision a person should see: what leads, what was cut, which proof and why"]}

Invented example of the SHAPE only:
{"kind": "design", "theme": null, "subject": "...", "preview": "...", "sections": [{"s": "band"}, {"s": "hero_type", "eyebrow": "...", "headline": "... <i>...</i>", "picture": {"stage": "product:<name>", "alt": "...", "source": "cut"}}, {"s": "offer", "price": "...", "was": "...", "cta": "..."}, {"s": "foot"}], "notes": ["..."]}

section and a scene still are all sent as this, in this order, with different

different prompt even when every value matches. A slot with nothing in it is
left out entirely — never sent as an empty line, never filled with a guess.

3b · standing-rules-v1-owner.md
# The standing rules — on every picture, whatever it is for

These go on the end of every prompt this component sends. Each one is here
because a real picture failed without it.

A caller can add to them. A caller cannot take one away — that is what
"standing" means.

**Where each rule came from.** This table is documentation and is NOT sent to
the model; everything below the rule is.

| Rule | Came from | The failure it was written after |
|---|---|---|
| No invented text | `tools/email-production/simple_email.py` — "No words, letters, numbers or logos anywhere in the image." | A hero invented its own headline and argued with the real one underneath it. |
| The product is ours | `tools/image-production/static/tools/paths.py` `product_cutout` — "A generated tube is a different product wearing our name." | The judge correctly failed a generated product, 2026-08-31. |
| No other brand | `finish.py` STANDING_CHECKS | A competitor's wordmark legible in a paid frame. |
| Nothing grossly broken | `finish.py` STANDING_CHECKS, narrowed 2026-09-05 on the owner's call | Finger-counting and micro-geometry killed good pictures and cost more than the defects they caught — so this is deliberately coarse. |
| No equipment in frame | `prompt.py`, the C2 split | "Shot on a phone on a tripod" put a phone on a tripod in the middle of a barbershop. |
| Surface truth | `style-packs.json` `texture`, on every pack | A phone photo of a real person came back looking like a campaign, which is a different ad. |
| One coherent object | `brand_facts.py` PLAIN_PRODUCT_CHECK | A product whose parts changed between appearances in one frame. |

---

STANDING RULES — these hold for this picture whatever else is asked above.

1. NO INVENTED TEXT. Do not render any words, letters, numbers, captions,
labels, callouts, watermarks, subtitles or user-interface furniture anywhere in
the frame. If words belong in this picture they are named in the direction
above, spelled exactly as written there, and nothing else is spelled at all.

2. THE PRODUCT IS OURS OR IT IS ABSENT. Where the product appears it is the
object described or attached above — the same pack, the same proportions, the
same colours, the same label. Do not redraw it, restyle it, relabel it, improve
it or invent a second version of it. If you cannot render the real object,
leave it out of frame rather than approximate it.

3. NO OTHER BRAND. No third-party or competitor brand name, logo, wordmark,
packaging or storefront is legible anywhere in the frame.

4. NOTHING GROSSLY BROKEN. No limb attached wrongly, no melted face, no body
with the wrong number of arms. Judge this the way a viewer scrolling past
would: a partly hidden hand, a foreshortened grip or an odd-looking finger is
fine and is not what this rule is about.

5. NO EQUIPMENT IN FRAME. Describe the result, never the apparatus. A camera, a
phone, a tripod, a ring light or a lighting rig appears in frame only when the
direction above puts it there on purpose.

6. SURFACE TRUTH. Skin keeps its pores, follicles, marks and micro-shadow;
surfaces keep their grain. Nothing is smoothed, beautified, airbrushed or made
cleaner than the thing it is a picture of.

7. ONE COHERENT OBJECT. Anything that appears more than once in the frame is
the same object each time — same parts, same marks, same label.

# The judge — one finished picture, checked before anyone sees it

Sent to a vision model with the picture attached. The tests are assembled per
picture: the standing ones, the brand's own product tests (read from
`brands/<brand>/element-facts.json`, never typed here), the purpose's extras,
and whatever the caller added.

The hedge clause is the load-bearing part: a picture nobody can confirm is not
a picture that passed.

---

You are checking one finished picture before it ships. The image is attached.

Answer EVERY test below with PASS or FAIL, then one short sentence of the
evidence you actually saw. Judge only what is visible.

A hedge is a FAIL. "Probably fine", "mostly correct", "hard to tell" all mean
FAIL — a picture nobody can confirm is not a picture that passed. You are the
only gate before this reaches a paying feed, an inbox or a live page.

TESTS
